claims.text: The nanoparticles are equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt.
The initial nanoparticles form a disordered solid solution.
The proposed intervention heats the particles under vacuum from room temperature to 1000 K.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down below a critical particle-size threshold.
A sufficiently high surface-to-volume ratio causes surface-energy-driven segregation.
A sufficiently high surface-to-volume ratio causes Ostwald ripening to dominate over bulk thermodynamic stabilization.
Surface diffusion and interfacial-energy gradients drive atomic flux from high-curvature regions to low-curvature regions.
Surface-energy minimization kinetically dominates configurational-entropy stabilization during heating.
Heating produces rapid phase separation rather than uniformly sluggish diffusion.
Selective evaporation contributes to the loss of the smallest particles.
Coalescence or Ostwald ripening contributes to the loss of the smallest particles.
Particles smaller than 5 nm disappear or coalesce into larger aggregates.
The resulting larger aggregates have irregular, anisotropic shapes.
Au and Pt are lower-surface-energy constituents in this alloy system.
Au and Pt segregate to the surfaces of the remaining larger particles.
High entropy of mixing and sluggish bulk diffusion theoretically predict uniform thermal stability and retention of equiatomic composition.
The hypothesis applies strictly to particles with diameters below 10 nm.
For particles larger than 20 nm, bulk thermodynamics may dominate surface effects and the sluggish-diffusion model may remain valid.
The exact critical size for transition to surface-driven behavior is unknown.
Experimental data for this quinary system under the specified heating conditions are lacking.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is stated to apply strictly below 10 nm, but the falsification rule partly depends on behavior of particles above 15 nm; that comparator is not clearly within the claimed operating regime, and the boundary only discusses particles above 20 nm.

Selective evaporation, particle coalescence, and Ostwald ripening are presented as interchangeable explanations for particle loss, although they are distinct mass-transport mechanisms and would yield different material-balance and trajectory signatures.
